evidence.quote: We interviewed between two to seven close relations of each of 12 men who died by suicide.
This paper focuses on suicides of 12 men because we gained information about each suicide from multiple participants (two to seven close relatives and friends).
The setting for the study was Accra, the capital of Ghana with an urban population of 2.27 million (Ghana Statistical Service, 2012).
We sought permission and assistance from the police headquarters in Accra to obtain access to police suicide data and bereaved families.
We interviewed between two to seven close relations of each of 12 men who died by suicide.

We purposively sampled 15 certified suicides that occurred in Accra and its environs between 2014 and 2015 by persons aged 15 years and above. There were 14 men, all Christians. This paper focuses on suicides of 12 men because we gained information about each suicide from multiple participants (two to seven close relatives and friends). We selected 43 close relations and friends (hereafter participants) of the deceased persons through purposeful and snowballing techniques.
To some of these deceased men, breach of patriarchal norms occurred through role reversal and fear of marital loss. This state of affairs seemed to have contributed to their suicides.

Physical illness that threatened sexual potency in two men seems to have contributed to the suicides. On the eve of a surgery related to a urological illness, one man killed himself. A sibling said, "He told me point blank that he was scared so he didn't go there."

Our findings, arising from accounts of persons who were close to men who killed themselves in Ghana, thus add another perspective to the influence of economic factors in male suicides similar to that of Kizza et al. (2012) in Uganda.

We interviewed between two to seven close relations of each of 12 men who died by suicide. Interpretative phenomenological analysis of data indicates that experiences of shame related to loss of economic control, breach of patriarchal norms, and threats to sexual competence contributed to the suicides.

We purposively sampled 15 certified suicides that occurred in Accra and its environs between 2014 and 2015 by persons aged 15 years and above. We selected 43 close relations and friends (hereafter participants) of the deceased persons through purposeful and snowballing techniques.
The first author (a native Ghanaian) conducted all the interviews, which lasted between 25 min to 3.5 h and occurred between 3 to 18 months after the suicides.

Interpretative phenomenological analysis of data indicates that experiences of shame related to loss of economic control, breach of patriarchal norms, and threats to sexual competence contributed to the suicides. Addressing socioeconomic issues, creating opportunities for men to disclose their emotions, and identifying sources of these emotions may help prevent suicide among men.
These close relations indicated three main sources of shame that seemed important for the person who died by suicide.

One important theme (n ¼ 9) was loss of economic control. Attaining economic control seemed a precondition for fulfilling masculine aspirations of these men. One aspect of loss of economic control was constrained livelihood. Challenges with employment led to frustrations and distress for some of the men. For example, one friend reflected, "I was thinking it was because of frustration and stress which he went through due to the collapse of his once vibrant business." This friend connected negative affect with the collapsed business, which shattered a previous life anchored on business success. His spouse said, "Life became very difficult to bear at that time, he was owing the suppliers." The job loss had consequences in the family domain.
To some of these deceased men, breach of patriarchal norms occurred through role reversal and fear of marital loss. This state of affairs seemed to have contributed to their suicides.

A third theme was threat to sexual competence due to fear of losing sexual potency and loss of respect due to childlessness. Physical illness that threatened sexual potency in two men seems to have contributed to the suicides. On the eve of a surgery related to a urological illness, one man killed himself.

These 43 people described the circumstances surrounding their close relations' suicidal death in Ghana in three themes: shame about losing economic control, breach of patriarchal norms, and a threat to sexual competence.
